families.name: London System: 1...Nf6
families.idea: The same pyramid against 1...Nf6. What changes is the ...g6 and ...d6 set-ups: h3 saves your bishop from ...Nh5, Be2 replaces Bd3, and when ...e5 comes the bishop drops to h2 and c4 takes space.
masters: Against King's Indian set-ups the London is at its most flexible: White can choose between the pyramid and a c4 plan after seeing what Black does.

families.name: London System: other first moves
families.idea: Every other reply to 1.d4. Most of them transpose to the pyramid after 2.Bf4; 1...c5 gets 2.d5, and 1...e5 is the Englund Gambit, where one trap decides everything.
masters: The Englund Gambit is unsound, but its trap has won a huge number of games at club level, so learning the single correct reply is worth your time.

families.name: Jobava London
families.idea: Nc3 and Bf4 instead of the pyramid. The knight blocks the c-pawn but aims at b5, where with the bishop it hits c7. If Black trades bishops on d3, recapture with the c-pawn for control of e4 and c4, the c-file and b3 for the queen.
masters: Named after the Georgian grandmaster Baadur Jobava, and also called the Rapport-Jobava system after Richard Rapport, who has also used it at elite level.
Compared with the pyramid London it is sharper and asks Black concrete questions from move three: ...c5 and ...Be7 both run into Nb5.

families.name: Caro-Kann: Advance
families.idea: White gets space with 3.e5. Your bishop goes to f5 before ...e6, then ...c5 and ...Qb6 attack the d4 chain from its base, and ...Ne7 goes to f5 or g6.
masters: Short and Tal popularised two very different White plans here: the quiet Nf3 and Be2, and the h4 and g4 pawn chase.

families.name: Caro-Kann: Exchange and Panov
families.idea: After 3.exd5 cxd5 the structure is symmetrical. Develop with ...Nc6, ...Nf6, ...Bg4 and ...e6, and against c4 (the Panov) blockade the isolated d-pawn and swap pieces.
masters: Botvinnik played the Panov as White in his world title matches, so its isolated-pawn plans are some of the best studied of all.

families.name: Caro-Kann: other White systems
families.idea: Everything else: the Two Knights, 2.Nf3, 2.Bc4, 2.f4, the King's Indian Attack with 2.d3, 2.c4, 2.e5 and the Fantasy with 3.f3. The reply is nearly always ...d5, then the same bishop-first development.
masters: Bobby Fischer played the Two Knights with 3.Nf3 against the Caro-Kann, and ...Bg4 is still the principled reply.

london-kid.name: London System vs the King's Indian set-up
london-kid.idea: Against ...g6 and ...Bg7, keep the London shell with two adjustments: h3 saves your bishop from ...Nh5, and Be2 is better than Bd3, which would only hit a solid g6 pawn. Black's play comes from ...c5 and ...e5.
notes: Centre pawn.
Black develops and keeps options open.
The London move order: bishop out first.
King's Indian set-up.
Support d4 and open the f1-bishop.
The bishop goes to the long diagonal.
Develop and control e5.
Black castles.
Modest but right: on d3 it would hit a solid g6.
Prepare ...e5 or ...c5.
Give the bishop h2 against ...Nh5.
Black hits d4.
The pyramid again.
Black develops and adds pressure to d4.
Castle. Plan: Nbd2, Re1 or Qb3, keep d4 solid.
why: You start with the queen's pawn and claim the centre. In the London you build the same set-up against almost anything Black plays, so your first moves are about piece placement rather than move-order theory.

Black develops and controls e4 without committing the d-pawn. Black can still choose ...d5 lines, a King's Indian set-up with ...g6, or ...e6 ideas, so you want a move that is useful against all of them.

You play the London straight away. Bf4 is useful against every Black set-up and avoids the long theory that 2.c4 invites. If Black plays ...d5 you transpose to the normal London; against ...g6 you get the line studied here.
Black prepares ...Bg7 and ...O-O, letting you have the centre for now and planning to hit it later with ...c5 or ...e5. The fianchettoed bishop will aim along the long diagonal at d4 and b2.
The usual London move. Your d4 pawn will need support against the coming ...c5, and e3 provides it while opening a diagonal for the f1-bishop. The f4-bishop stays outside the chain.
From g7 the bishop aims down the long diagonal. Right now its own knight on f6 blocks it, but once that knight moves (for example ...Nh5 or ...Nd7), d4 and b2 come under fire.
The knight develops, covers e5 against a later ...e5 break and prepares castling. The e5 square is where Black's King's Indian plan hits you, so every piece that controls it matters.
Black's king is safe, and Black now chooses a plan: ...d6 with ...c5 or ...e5, or ...d5 for a more Grünfeld-like centre. Your set-up stays the same, so keep developing.
Against a fianchetto the bishop on d3 has no target, because h7 is covered by the g6 pawn and the king. On e2 it also avoids a later ...e5-e4, which would hit a d3-bishop and the f3-knight together.
Black prepares the King's Indian break ...e5 and keeps ...c5 in reserve. The f6-knight also has ...Nh5 to chase your f4-bishop, so it is time to give the bishop a retreat.

A key London detail against ...g6: if Black plays ...Nh5, your bishop can drop back to h2 and keep its diagonal instead of being swapped for a knight. The h3 pawn also takes g4 from Black's knight and bishop.
Black challenges your centre from the side, the same idea as against the normal London. Once the f6-knight moves, the g7-bishop will add to the pressure on d4 and b2, so you reinforce the centre now.
The c3 pawn adds a second pawn guard to d4, so the g7-bishop will meet a wall. Black's most testing reply is ...Qb6, hitting b2; meet it with Qb3, offering a queen trade.
The knight joins the c5 pawn in attacking d4, while the g7-bishop is still blocked by its own knight. Your d4 pawn is defended by c3, e3, Nf3 and the queen, so it holds.

Your king is safe and development is nearly done. Next come Nbd2 and Re1 or Qb3, keeping d4 solid. If Black exchanges with ...cxd4, recapture exd4 to keep a pawn on d4 and open the e-file for your rook.

gm.8: Principle: put a bishop where it has targets. Against a fianchetto the h7 pawn is covered, so the modest e2 square serves the bishop better than d3.
gm.10: London players treat h3 against ...g6 set-ups as close to automatic: losing the f4-bishop to ...Nh5 gives up the London's best piece.

carokann-adv.name: Caro-Kann: Advance Variation (Short System)
carokann-adv.idea: Against 3.e5, develop the bishop to f5 before ...e6, then hit the base of White's chain with ...c5 and pile on d4 and e5 with your knights.
notes: King's pawn.
Prepare ...d5 with a pawn behind it.
White takes the full centre.
Challenge e4.
The Advance: White grabs space.
Bishop out before ...e6 locks it in.
White develops and supports d4 and e5.
Build the chain; the bishop is already outside.
Quiet development: White castles next.
Strike the base of White's chain.
White props up d4 with a piece.
The knight eyes e5 and covers c5.
White castles.
Heading for c6 via e7.
White reinforces d4 with a pawn.
Now both knights hit e5.
White develops the last minor piece.
Develop and get ready to castle.
why: White occupies the centre and opens diagonals for the queen and light-squared bishop. You meet it with the Caro-Kann, which prepares ...d5 with a pawn behind it so your centre stays solid whatever White does.
Prepare ...d5 and keep the c8-bishop's diagonal open, the big difference from the French. In this line you will get that bishop to f5 before ...e6, so it ends up outside your pawn chain.
White builds the classic two-pawn centre on d4 and e4. If you stay passive, White uses the space to cramp you, so you challenge e4 at once with ...d5, the move the Caro-Kann prepared.
You attack e4. White can defend it with a knight, exchange on d5, or push past with e5. Each choice changes the pawn structure, and this line covers the push, a very popular choice at club level.

The Advance Variation. White gains space and takes f6 from your king's knight, but the e5-pawn can become a target. Your plan is to undermine the chain with ...c5, which here costs an extra tempo because the c-pawn has already moved.

Get the bishop out to f5 before ...e6 shuts it in. It eyes e4, d3 and c2 and is far more active than its French cousin. White's sharpest try is 4.Nc3 with g4 to chase it, but the calm 4.Nf3 is what you will meet most.

White develops quietly and supports both d4 and e5. This is the Short System: no pawn storm, just solid development, castling and using the extra space. It is less sharp than 4.Nc3 but full of strategic content.
Now ...e6 is ideal: it supports d5 and opens the f8-bishop, while the light-squared bishop already stands outside on f5. Your pawns on d5 and e6 face White's chain on d4 and e5.
White develops the bishop modestly and prepares to castle. From e2 it supports later ideas such as c4 to open the c-file or Nh4 to hit your bishop on f5.
Strike the base of the pawn chain. The d4-pawn holds up e5, so pressure on d4 is pressure on the whole structure. It costs a second move with the c-pawn, but White's quiet set-up gives you the time.
White defends d4 with a piece instead of c3. If you take on d4, Nxd4 gives White a strong central knight that also hits your bishop on f5, so you usually keep the tension for now.
The knight comes to d7 to fight for e5 and to recapture on c5 if White ever plays dxc5. Keeping the tension means White must keep worrying about d4.
White castles and keeps a flexible position. Options include c3 to fix the centre, c4 to open the c-file, or Nbd2 and Nb3 to put pressure on c5.
Your king's knight cannot use f6 because of the e5-pawn, so it travels via e7 to c6, where it presses on d4. Keeping the f-pawn free also leaves ...f6 available later to undermine e5.
White adds a pawn to d4's defence so the chain is secure. The downside is that the b1-knight loses c3 and must come out via d2 or a3.
The knight arrives on c6. Together with the d7-knight it eyes e5, and with the c5-pawn it presses d4. If White ever plays dxc5, recapturing leaves the e5-pawn lonely and weak.
White develops the last minor piece. From d2 the knight can go to b3 to hit c5, or support the kingside if the f3-knight moves. White has finished developing, so the fight over e5 and d4 begins.
Develop and prepare to castle. Plans: ...O-O, then either ...cxd4 and ...Qb6 against b2 and d4, or ...f6 to open the f-file against e5. The position is balanced and full of play for both sides.

gm.6: This quiet set-up with Nf3 and Be2 is named after Nigel Short, who made it popular at the top level. It avoids heavy theory and simply plays on White's extra space.
gm.9: Nimzowitsch taught that a pawn chain should be attacked at its base. Here the base is d4, so ...c5 is the thematic strike even though it spends a second tempo on the c-pawn.

carokann-g4.name: Caro-Kann: Advance, 4.g4?!
carokann-g4.idea: White chases the f5-bishop with pawns. Step to e4, drop back to g6, and answer h4 with 6...h5!, which stops h5 and leaves White's kingside full of holes. The natural 6...h6? allows 7.h5 Bh7 8.e6! and a strong attack.
notes: King's pawn.
Prepare ...d5 with a pawn behind it.
White takes the full centre.
Challenge e4.
The Advance: White grabs space.
Bishop out before ...e6 locks it in.
White chases the bishop with a pawn.
Hit the h1-rook first.
White blocks the bishop with a pawn.
Retreat; the bishop is safe on g6.
White threatens h5 to bury the bishop.
Stop h5. Not 6...h6? 7.h5 and 8.e6!
White heads for f4.
Solid: open the f8-bishop.
The knight eyes g6 and h5.
Develop and guard g6.
White develops.
Open the h-file.
White recaptures.
Keep the bishop; ...c5 next.
why: White occupies the centre and opens diagonals for the queen and light-squared bishop. You meet it with the Caro-Kann, which prepares ...d5 with a pawn behind it so your centre stays solid whatever White does.

White builds the classic two-pawn centre on d4 and e4. If you stay passive, White uses the space to cramp you, so you challenge e4 at once with ...d5, the move the Caro-Kann prepared.
You attack e4. White can defend it with a knight, exchange on d5, or push past with e5. Each choice changes the pawn structure, and this line covers the push, a very popular choice at club level.

The Advance Variation. White gains space and takes f6 from your king's knight, but the e5-pawn can become a target. Your plan is to undermine the chain with ...c5, which here costs an extra tempo because the c-pawn has already moved.

Get the bishop out to f5 before ...e6 shuts it in. It eyes e4, d3 and c2 and is far more active than its French cousin. White's sharpest try is 4.Nc3 with g4 to chase it, but the calm 4.Nf3 is what you will meet most.
An aggressive club favourite. White wants to gain space with tempo and bury your bishop, but the pawn move also loosens White's whole kingside, and you will use that.
The bishop steps to e4 and attacks the h1-rook. White has to answer with f3, weakening the kingside further, before your bishop goes back.
White blocks with a pawn and gains another tempo, but the e3-square and the g1-a7 diagonal are now weak, and White's king will never feel fully safe.
Drop back to g6. The bishop is outside the pawn chain and cannot be trapped, because it can always come back to h7.
White threatens h5 to drive your bishop to h7, followed by tricks with e6. This is the moment to react precisely.

The key move: stop h4-h5 in its tracks. After the natural 6...h6? 7.h5 Bh7 8.e6! White breaks open your kingside with a big lead in space. With ...h5 you fix White's pawns and prepare to open the h-file for your rook.
The knight heads for f4, where it hits g6 and h5. White is trying to win back control of the kingside.
Build the usual chain and free your dark-squared bishop. The e6-pawn also rules out any e5-e6 pawn sacrifice.
The knight attacks the h5-pawn and eyes your bishop. White hopes to win the h-pawn or force the bishop to give itself up.
The knight develops and guards g6. It prepares ...Nd7 and ...c5, and later it may come to f5, a fine square in front of White's pawns.
White brings out the queenside knight. With the kingside pawns already committed, White cannot castle short safely.
Trade on g4 to open the h-file for your rook, which already sits on h8. White's h4-pawn becomes a long-term weakness.
White takes back with the f-pawn, which leaves e5 without the support of a pawn on f4 and makes e3 weaker still.
Tuck the bishop on h7, where it still controls the b1-h7 diagonal. Next come ...c5 and ...Nbc6 against d4. White has overextended, and engines prefer your position.

carokann-exch.name: Caro-Kann: Exchange Variation
carokann-exch.idea: A Queen's Gambit Exchange structure with colours reversed: develop actively with ...Nc6, ...Bg4 and ...e6, trade dark-squared bishops, then play the minority attack with ...b5-b4.
notes: King's pawn.
Prepare ...d5.
White takes the centre.
Challenge e4.
The Exchange: White releases the tension.
Recapture with the c-pawn.
White aims the bishop at h7.
Develop and pressure d4.
White supports d4.
Develop; the knight guards h7 and d5.
White's bishop takes the b8-h2 diagonal.
Develop with a hit on the queen.
White steps out and attacks b7.
Defend b7 along the seventh rank.
White develops and covers f3.
Open the f8-bishop.
White completes kingside development.
Offer the trade of dark-squared bishops.
White takes.
Recapture; plan ...O-O and ...b5-b4.
why: White claims the centre. Many club players choose the Exchange against the Caro-Kann to avoid theory and reach a quiet game, so it pays to know the plans well and play for more than a draw.
Prepare ...d5 with a pawn behind it. In the Exchange this matters directly: when White takes on d5 you recapture with the c-pawn and get a half-open c-file.
White builds the two-pawn centre on d4 and e4. You challenge it at once with ...d5, before White can use the space to push e5 and cramp your kingside pieces.
You strike at e4. White's quietest answer is to exchange on d5, which gives a symmetrical-looking structure. It is strategically rich, though, because the pawns on each wing are not balanced.
White releases the tension. The game opens a little, and White hopes for quick kingside pressure with Bd3, Bf4 and Qb3 or Qc2, using the extra tempo of the first move.
Recapture toward the centre with the c-pawn. You keep a pawn on d5 and open the c-file for your rooks, and your a- and b-pawns against White's a2, b2 and c3 will later give you a minority attack.
The bishop aims at h7 and controls f5, which stops your light-squared bishop from developing there comfortably. That is why you look to g4 for it instead, usually after ...Nc6 and ...Nf6.
Develop the knight and put pressure on d4. It also covers e5, so White's knight cannot settle there easily, and it can later jump to a5 to harass a white queen that comes to b3.
White supports d4 with a pawn, which also takes b4 and d4 away from your knight. The downside is that the b1-knight can no longer use c3, so it must develop via d2.
Develop and cover h7 against the bishop on d3. The knight on f6 also defends d5 and keeps an eye on e4, so White cannot easily gain space there.
White's bishop takes the b8-h2 diagonal before you can play ...e6 and ...Bd6. It also controls c7, so your queen cannot use that square, and it adds to White's grip on e5.
Develop the bishop outside the chain with tempo on the queen on d1. Because the d3-bishop covers f5, g4 is the active square. Later you can swap it for White's f3-knight, a key guard of e5.
White steps out of the attack with tempo on b7. Grabbing pawns with your queen here would be risky, so the question is how to defend b7 without losing time.

The queen guards b7 along the seventh rank and stays connected to the kingside. The alternative ...Na5 kicks the queen but sends the knight to the edge. You can also take on f3 when White's knight arrives there.
White develops and prepares Ngf3, so that if you take on f3 White can recapture with the d2-knight and keep the pawn structure intact. The c3 and d4 chain stays solid.
Open the diagonal for your dark-squared bishop and support d5. Your pawns on d5 and e6 form a solid wedge, and your light-squared bishop is already outside the chain on g4.
White finishes kingside development and is ready to castle. The knight on f3 eyes e5, the square White would most like to occupy, because a knight there would hit f7 and your queen on d7.

Offer to trade dark-squared bishops. White's bishop on f4 is a good piece that controls e5 and b8, and swapping it reduces White's attacking chances. If White retreats instead, you take over the b8-h2 diagonal.
White accepts the trade. Retreating with Bg3 keeps more pieces on, but the exchange is the main line and keeps the game simple for White. Now your queen recaptures and takes over the dark squares.

Recapture, and the dark squares are under your control. Plans: ...O-O, then ...Rab8 and ...b5-b4 to attack c3, the classic minority attack. Keep ...Bxf3 ready to remove the knight before it lands on e5.

gm.12: Bobby Fischer used this set-up with Bf4 and Qb3 to beat Tigran Petrosian in the 1970 USSR v Rest of the World match. Petrosian chose ...Na5; ...Qd7 is the calmer modern choice.
gm.19: This is the Carlsbad structure from the Queen's Gambit Exchange with colours reversed. There White's standard plan is the minority attack with b4-b5; here you play the mirror image with ...b5-b4.

carokann-twoknights.name: Caro-Kann: Two Knights Variation
carokann-twoknights.idea: White develops both knights before d4. Pin and take the f3-knight, put your pawns on light squares with ...e6, and use your good dark-squared bishop and the ...e5 or ...d4 breaks to free the game.
notes: King's pawn.
The Caro-Kann.
White develops instead of 2.d4.
Challenge e4 anyway.
The Two Knights: White keeps d4 in reserve.
Pin the f3-knight.
White asks the bishop to decide.
Give up the bishop for the knight.
White recaptures; the queen eyes f7.
Pawns to light squares; the dark bishop is free.
White keeps the centre closed and solid.
Develop and put a piece on e4.
White develops and prepares to castle.
Develop; the knight backs up ...e5.
White castles.
Your good bishop takes an active diagonal.
White's queen hits g7.
Castle; g7 is covered. Plan ...Qe7 and ...e5.
why: White opens with the king's pawn and you answer with the Caro-Kann. In this line White will avoid 2.d4 and develop knights first, hoping to keep the game away from your usual structures.
Prepare ...d5 with a pawn behind it, as always. Your c8-bishop's diagonal stays open, and in this line that bishop will go to g4 to fight White's knights.
White develops and protects e4 instead of building the d4 and e4 centre. The d-pawn stays flexible: it can go to d3 for a solid set-up or to d4 later.
Challenge e4 exactly as in the main lines. If White exchanges on d5 you recapture with the c-pawn and keep a pawn in the centre, and if White pushes e5 your bishop comes out freely.
The Two Knights. Both knights are out, e4 is held by the c3-knight, and White keeps options such as Bc4, Ne5 or a quiet d3. Your most reliable reply is to pin the f3-knight at once.
Pin the knight against the queen and develop the bishop before ...e6 shuts it in. Removing the f3-knight later weakens White's control of d4 and e5 and makes your central breaks stronger.
White asks the bishop to decide. Retreating with ...Bh5 lets White gain space with g4 and take the initiative, so the main line simply takes on f3 and gets on with development.
Give up the bishop for the knight. You hand White the bishop pair, but you gain time, and with your pawns about to stand on light squares, the bishop you keep on f8 will be the good one.
White recaptures with the queen, which now eyes f7 down the f-file and supports e4. White hopes the bishop pair will tell in the long run, so your job is to stay solid and develop quickly.
Support d5 against the e4-pawn and the c3-knight, and open the f8-bishop. Your pawns on c6, d5 and e6 now sit on light squares, so your dark-squared bishop is free to find an active post.

White chooses a solid set-up, keeping e4 protected by the pawn and avoiding an early d4 that would open lines. The plan is Be2 or g3 and Bg2, castling, and later kingside play with the bishop pair behind it.
Develop the knight and put a piece against e4. It also covers h7 and d5, which matters once White's queen and bishops turn toward your king, and it prepares castling.
White develops the last kingside piece and gets ready to castle short. The bishop on e2 looks modest, but it covers g4 and keeps the light squares near White's king under control.
Develop the knight to d7, where it supports a later ...e5 and can recapture on c5 or e5. Your queen stays flexible and can go to b6, c7 or e7 depending on White's set-up.
White castles short. White's ideas now include Qg3 to hit g7, Bh6 or Bf4 to bring the dark-squared bishop into play, and exd5 to open lines so the bishop pair gets more scope.

Put the bishop on its most active diagonal, aiming at f2 and the king on g1 and controlling d4. With your pawns on light squares this is your good bishop, so keep it active and avoid trading it cheaply.
White's queen attacks g7, which has no defender until you castle. White also prepares Bh6 or Bf4 to add pressure, so you need to deal with the kingside straight away.

Castle, which covers g7 with the king and makes your position safe. Plans: ...Qe7, ...Rae8 and the central break ...e5, or ...d4 to gain space. White's bishop pair is kept in check by your compact pawns.

gm.7: A common Caro-Kann trade-off: give up the light-squared bishop for a knight when your pawns are heading to light squares anyway. The bishop that stays behind is the good one, and the position stays compact.

carokann-bh5.name: Caro-Kann: Two Knights, 4...Bh5
carokann-bh5.idea: Keeping the bishop with 4...Bh5 is sharper than 4...Bxf3. After 5.exd5 cxd5 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.g4 Bg6 8.Ne5 you must defend c6 with 8...Rc8!. The natural 8...e6?? loses material to 9.Nxc6, and even after the right move you have to defend precisely.
notes: King's pawn.
The Caro-Kann.
White develops instead of 2.d4.
Challenge e4 anyway.
The Two Knights: White keeps d4 in reserve.
Pin the f3-knight.
White asks the bishop to decide.
Keep the bishop: the sharper choice.
White opens the position.
Recapture with the pawn.
Check: White targets c6.
Block with the knight.
White chases the bishop.
Retreat to g6.
The knight hits c6 a second time.
Defend c6. Not 8...e6?? 9.Nxc6!
White builds the centre.
Now ...e6 is safe.
White threatens h5 to trap the bishop.

Prepare ...d5 with a pawn behind it, as always. Your c8-bishop's diagonal stays open, and in this line that bishop will go to g4 to fight White's knights.

Challenge e4 exactly as in the main lines. If White exchanges on d5 you recapture with the c-pawn and keep a pawn in the centre, and if White pushes e5 your bishop comes out freely.
The Two Knights. Both knights are out, e4 is held by the c3-knight, and White keeps options such as Bc4, Ne5 or a quiet d3. Your most reliable reply is to pin the f3-knight at once.
Pin the knight against the queen and develop the bishop before ...e6 shuts it in. Removing the f3-knight later weakens White's control of d4 and e5 and makes your central breaks stronger.
White asks the bishop to decide. Taking on f3 is the simple main line. Keeping the bishop is more ambitious but lets White chase it with g4.
You keep the bishop and the pin. White will now try to win time against it with g4 and Ne5, so you must know the next few moves exactly.
White exchanges, opening the a4-e8 diagonal towards your king before you have castled.
Take back with the c-pawn and keep a pawn in the centre. The a4-e8 diagonal is now open, so a check on b5 is coming.
The check forces a block, and the blocking piece will become a target once White's knight lands on e5.
Block with the knight and develop. Now c6 is pinned against your king, so keep counting its attackers and defenders.
White gains space and drives your bishop off the pin, accepting holes on the kingside in return.
Drop back to g6, where the bishop is safe and eyes the b1-h7 diagonal.
The knight attacks the pinned c6-knight a second time and also eyes your g6-bishop. This is where most players go wrong.

Defend c6 with the rook. The natural 8...e6?? drops material to 9.Nxc6! bxc6 10.Bxc6+, which checks your king and attacks the a8-rook at the same time. Count the attackers on a pinned piece before you develop.
White grabs the centre and frees the c1-bishop. The pressure on c6 stays, so keep it defended.
With c6 covered by the rook, you can play ...e6 at last and open the f8-bishop.
White threatens h5, which would trap the g6-bishop. You need to give it a way out or let it be traded.
Hit the e5-knight so it has to decide. After a trade on g6 you recapture with the h-pawn, which opens the h-file for your rook.
White gets the bishop pair. In return your h-file is open and White's g4 and h4 pawns are loose.
Take back towards the centre and open the h-file. Your rook on h8 now presses on h4.
The queen attacks the g6-pawn and eyes the light squares around your king. You need to protect g6 once more.
The king defends g6 and is safer on f7 than it looks, behind a wall of pawns. Engines rate the position about equal, but it is double-edged. If you want a calm game, choose 4...Bxf3 instead.
